instructions.content: Never reproduce the actual 'Cunk' character name, her real interview lines, or any specific real broadcast segment verbatim or near-verbatim; use an original, unnamed or differently named presenter character instead.
Never let the presenter acknowledge their own ignorance or break deadpan; the comedy depends on total, unbroken sincerity.
Never make the expert's answers exasperated or hostile; the expert's strained but patient sincerity is what makes the presenter's ignorance land as absurd rather than cruel.
Never let an escalation happen through the presenter's delivery instead of the content; confidence must stay flat while only the claims get worse.

Never let the presenter's confidently wrong claim turn out to be secretly correct as a 'gotcha' twist; a hidden correct answer implies the presenter knew better all along, which collapses the sincere-ignorance premise retroactively.

Pick a subject with real-world weight (history, science, art, technology, civic institutions) before drafting narration, since sincere misunderstanding of something people take seriously is what lands as funny.

Structure a segment as scene-setting narration followed by a cutaway interview with a credentialed expert, escalate each beat to be slightly more wrong than the last, then close on a pseudo-profound one-liner that is actually trivial or meaningless.
Favour short, declarative sentences delivered with total certainty over long comic set-pieces.
Either escalate wrongness gradually across a whole segment, or front-load one large misunderstanding and explore its implications afterward; both are valid depending on requested length.
